claims.evidence: This is a direct statement from the Materials and methods section describing the participant demographics and experimental procedure.

claims.claim: Data of four participants were omitted from further analyses due to excessive head movements (>3 mm or 3 degrees).
claims.source: Data of four participants were omitted from further analyses due to excessive head movements (>3 mm or 3 degrees).
claims.evidence: This is a direct statement about data exclusion criteria applied in the study.

claims.claim: The replication dataset came from 30 healthy older adults (12 males, aged 53–75 y) recruited from the residential community near the college.
claims.source: The replication dataset came from 30 healthy older adults (12 males, aged 53–75 y) recruited from the residential community near the college.
claims.evidence: This is a direct statement describing the replication dataset participant demographics.

claims.claim: After omitting 10 runs with large head movements (>3 mm or 3 degrees), a total of 50 runs of fMRI scans were included for subsequence analyses in the replication dataset.
claims.source: After omitting 10 runs with large head movements (>3 mm or 3 degrees), a total of 50 runs of fMRI scans were included for subsequence analyses.
claims.evidence: This is a direct statement about data exclusion and final sample size for the replication dataset.

claims.claim: The model with K = 3 achieved the best overall performance, quantified by summed z scores.
claims.source: The model with K = 3 achieved the best overall performance, quantified by summed z scores (Figure 1).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by the results shown in Figure 1 and described in the text, showing that K=3 had the highest summed z-score.

claims.claim: When applying a different whole-brain parcellation scheme (Yeo-7 Networks atlas) to extract the brain time series used for HMM inference, the model with K = 3 was found to be optimal.
claims.source: When applying a different whole-brain parcellation scheme (Yeo-7 Networks atlas) to extract the brain time series used for HMM inference, we also found the model with K = 3 to be the optimal (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by the replication analysis using a different parcellation scheme, shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claims.claim: When examining the replication dataset wherein participants' age, narrative contents, as well as scanning duration differed substantially from those of the main dataset, the model with K = 3 was found to be optimal.
claims.source: Moreover, when examining the replication dataset wherein participants' age, narrative contents, as well as scanning duration differed substantially from those of the main dataset, we again found the model with K = 3 to be optimal (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by the replication analysis on the older adult dataset, shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claims.claim: State #1 was characterized by relatively high activities in the auditory and somatomotor networks, along with low activities in the DMN and the cognitive control network.
claims.source: The first state (State #1) was characterized by relatively high activities in the auditory and somatomotor networks, along with low activities in the DMN and the cognitive control network (Figure 2).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by the activity patterns shown in Figure 2.

claims.claim: State #2 was characterized by relatively high activities in the language and the frontal-parietal networks whereas low activities in the somatomotor and auditory networks.
claims.source: The second state (State #2) was characterized by relatively high activities in the language and the frontal-parietal networks whereas low activities in the somatomotor and auditory networks, seemingly being associated with the basic linguistic component.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by the activity patterns shown in Figure 2.

claims.claim: State #3 was characterized by relatively high activities in the DMN and frontal-parietal networks whereas low activities in the auditory and language networks.
claims.source: The third state (State #3) was characterized by relatively high activities in the DMN and frontal-parietal networks whereas low activities in the auditory and language networks, seemingly being associated with the internal conceptual-intentional component.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by the activity patterns shown in Figure 2.

claims.claim: Both State #1 and State #3 were more likely to switch to State #2 than switching directly to each other.
claims.source: Consistent with our prediction, both State #1 and #3 were more likely to switch to State #2 than switching directly to each other, i.e., State #2 acted as a transitional hub.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by the between-state transition probability analysis shown in Figure 2.

claims.claim: The differences in transition probabilities observed in the experiment, computed as P(State#1→State#2)－P(State#1→State#3) and P(State#3→State#2)－P(State#3→State#1), were respectively larger than 99.9% and 94.4% of instances from the surrogate data.
claims.source: The results showed the differences in transition probabilities observed in our experiment, computed as P(State#1→State#2)－P(State#1→State#3) and P(State#3→State#2)－ P(State#3→State#1), were respectively larger than 99.9% and 94.4% of instances from the surrogate data (Figure 2).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by permutation testing results comparing observed transition probabilities to surrogate data.

claims.claim: The brain spent most of the time on State #2 (mean FO = 46.7%), next on State #1 (mean FO = 29%) and the least on State #3 (mean FO = 24.3%).
claims.source: In agreement with the between-state switching pattern, the brain spent most of the time on State #2 (mean FO = 46.7%), next on State #1 (mean FO = 29%) and the least on State #3 (mean FO = 24.3 %).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by the fractional occupancy (FO) measurements from the HMM analysis.

claims.claim: The dwelling time was 15.29 s for State #2, 9.99 s for State #1, and 9.68 s for State #3.
claims.source: The same pattern was found in the dwelling time, with a group mean of 15.29 s for State #2, 9.99 s for State #1, and 9.68 s for State #3.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by the dwell time measurements from the HMM analysis.

claims.claim: Both the FO and dwell time of State #2 were higher than 99.88% of instances in the surrogate data.
claims.source: Both the FO and dwell time of State #2 were higher than 99.88% of instances in the surrogate data.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by permutation testing comparing observed FO and dwell time to surrogate data.

claims.claim: When occupied by State #2, the brain exhibited significantly higher global efficiency than when occupied by the other two states (t values >4.67, ps <10–4).
claims.source: Consistent with our prediction, when occupied by State #2, the brain exhibited significantly higher global efficiency than when occupied by the other two states (t values >4.67, ps <10–4).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by graph theoretical analysis results shown in Figure 2.

claims.claim: When occupied by State #2, the brain exhibited significantly lower network modularity than when occupied by the other two states (t values <–5.82, ps <10–6).
claims.source: An opposite pattern was found in network modularity (t values <–5.82, ps <10–6).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by graph theoretical analysis results shown in Figure 2.

claims.claim: The correlation between speech envelope and the expression probability of State #1 was significantly greater than zero (t(63) = 2.67, p = 0.009, FDR corrected) with a group mean of 0.035.
claims.source: We observed a consistent positive correlation between the speech envelope and the expression probability of State #1 across participants, with a group mean of 0.035. This correlation was significantly greater than zero (t(63) = 2.67, p = 0.009, FDR corrected) and surpassed 99.8% of the 5,000 instances from permutation tests where the state time courses were randomly circularly shifted, yielding a mean of −0.0005 (Figure 3).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by correlation analysis and permutation testing shown in Figure 3.

claims.claim: The correlation between speech envelope and the expression probability of State #2 was significant with a group mean r=0.034 (t(63) = 2.61, p = 0.011, FDR corrected).
claims.source: A similar effect was observed for State #2, with a group mean r=0.034 (t(63) = 2.61, p = 0.011, FDR corrected).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by correlation analysis shown in Figure 3.

claims.claim: Only the expression probability of State #2 showed a consistent correlation with word-level semantic coherence across participants, with a group mean of 0.030 (one-sample t-test against zero: t(63) = 2.48, p = 0.015, FDR corrected).
claims.source: Among the three states, only the expression probability of State #2 showed a consistent correlation with word-level semantic coherence across participants, with a group mean of 0.030 (one-sample t-test against zero: t(63) = 2.48, p = 0.015, FDR corrected).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by correlation analysis shown in Figure 3.

claims.claim: The group mean correlation between word-level semantic coherence and State #2 expression was significantly greater than 99.28% of instances from permutation tests, which produced a mean r = 0.001.
claims.source: This group's mean value was significantly greater than 99.28% of instances from permutation tests, which produced a mean r = 0.001.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by permutation testing results.

claims.claim: Only the expression probability of State #3 exhibited a consistent correlation with clause-level semantic coherence, with a group mean of 0.031 (one-sample t-test against zero: t(63) = 2.89, p = 0.005, FDR corrected).
claims.source: Among the three states, only the expression probability of State #3 exhibited a consistent correlation with clause-level semantic coherence, with a group mean of 0.031 (one-sample t-test against zero: t(63) = 2.89, p = 0.005, FDR corrected).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by correlation analysis shown in Figure 3.

claims.claim: The group mean correlation between clause-level semantic coherence and State #3 expression was significantly greater than 99.8% of instances from the permuted data, which yielded a mean r = 0.0001.
claims.source: This group's mean value was significantly greater than 99.8% of instances from the permuted data, which yielded a mean r = 0.0001.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by permutation testing results.

claims.claim: Alignments with the best performers in both State #1 and State #2 were significantly correlated with participants' comprehension scores (Pearson's r(54) = 0.31 and 0.37, respectively).
claims.source: As anticipated, alignments with the best performers in both the State #1 and State #2 were significantly correlated with participants' comprehension scores (Pearson's r(54) = 0.31 and 0.37, respectively).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by correlation analysis shown in Figure 4.

claims.claim: A marginally significant correlation was found between alignment with the best performer in State #3 and comprehension scores (r(54) = 0.22, p = 0.10).
claims.source: A marginally significant correlation was also found in the alignment of State #3 (r(54) = 0.22, p = 0.10).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by correlation analysis.

claims.claim: Individual-to-group alignments were correlated with comprehension scores in all three states (r(62) = 0.42, 0.51, 0.27 for State #1, #2, and #3, respectively).
claims.source: Even stronger correlations were found between individual-to-group alignments and comprehension scores in all three states (r(62) = 0.42, 0.51, 0.27 for State #1, #2, and #3, respectively; Figure 4).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by correlation analysis shown in Figure 4.

claims.claim: Similarities with the best performers in terms of head movement trajectory were positively correlated with participants' comprehension scores (r(54) = 0.33, p = 0.01).
claims.source: Congruent with our assumption, similarities with the best performers in terms of head movement trajectory were indeed positively correlated with participants' comprehension scores (r(54) = 0.33, p = 0.01; Figure 4).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by correlation analysis shown in Figure 4.

claims.claim: After adjusting for head movement effects using partial correlation, the positive correlations between inter-brain alignment with the best performers and comprehension scores remained significant for State #1 (partial r(53) = 0.30, p = 0.03) and State #2 (partial r(53) = 0.31, p = 0.025), except for State #3 (partial r(53) = 0.12, p = 0.39).
claims.source: After adjusting the effect of head movement by applying partial correlation, the positive correlations between the inter-brain alignment with the best performers and comprehension scores remained significant for State #1 (partial r(53) = 0.30, p = 0.03) and State #2 (partial r(53) = 0.31, p = 0.025), except for State #3 (partial r(53) = 0.12, p = 0.39).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by partial correlation analysis controlling for head movement.

claims.claim: No significant correlation was found between individual differences in the FO and dwell time of latent states and individual differences in narrative comprehension (r values <0.15, ps >0.23).
claims.source: As a comparison, we investigated whether individual differences in the FO and dwell time of latent states were associated with individual differences in narrative comprehension. No significant result was found on any of the three states (r values <0.15, ps >0.23).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by correlation analysis showing no significant relationship.

claims.claim: In the older-adult dataset, no significant positive correlations were found between inter-subject alignment in brain states and narrative comprehension.
claims.source: However, in the dataset of older adults, we did not find significant positive correlations between inter-subject alignment in brain states and narrative comprehension.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by the analysis of the replication dataset shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claims.claim: ISCs among older adults were significantly lower than those among younger adults for all three states (For State #1: t(63, 49) = 3.32, p = 0.001; for State #2: t(63, 49) = 3.94, p < 0.001; and for State #3: t(63, 49) = 11.96, p < 10–6).
claims.source: For all three states, the ISCs were significantly higher among the young adults than that among the older adults. For State #1: t(63, 49) = 3.32, p = 0.001; for State #2: t(63, 49) = 3.94, p < 0.001; and for State #3: t(63, 49) = 11.96, p < 10–6.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by the comparison of ISCs between age groups shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claims.claim: During the rest period, State #3 acted as the transitional hub.
claims.source: Analysis of the between-state transition matrix revealed that, unlike in the task condition, State #3 acted as the transitional hub in the resting condition (Figure 5a).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by the between-state transition analysis shown in Figure 5a.

claims.claim: When listening to the unintelligible narrative (in Mongolian, MG), State #2 was still the transitional hub.
claims.source: Consistent with the task condition, State #2 served as the transitional hub under the MG condition (Figure 5b).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by the between-state transition analysis shown in Figure 5b.

claims.claim: The FOs of State #2 monotonically increased across the three conditions: resting < MG (incomprehensible speech) < task (narrative comprehension).
claims.source: Notably, the FOs of State #2 monotonically increased across the three conditions: resting < MG (incomprehensible speech) < task (narrative comprehension).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by the comparison of fractional occupancy across conditions shown in Figure 5c.

claims.claim: The FOs of State #3 monotonically decreased across the three conditions: resting > MG > task.
claims.source: In contrast, the FOs of the State #3 monotonically decreased: resting > MG > task (Figure 5c).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by the comparison of fractional occupancy across conditions shown in Figure 5c.

claims.claim: A similar pattern to FO was found on the dwelling time across the three conditions.
claims.source: A similar pattern was found on the dwelling time.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by the comparison of dwelling time across conditions shown in Figure 5c.

claims.claim: Speech comprehension involves the dynamic interplay of multiple cognitive processes, from basic sound perception, to linguistic encoding, and finally to complex semantic-conceptual interpretations.
claims.source: Speech comprehension involves the dynamic interplay of multiple cognitive processes, from basic sound perception, to linguistic encoding, and finally to complex semantic-conceptual interpretations.
claims.evidence: This is a statement in the Abstract summarizing the theoretical framework of the study.

claims.claim: The basic design of language faculty mainly comprises three modules (components): an external sensory-motor module, an internal conceptual-intentional module, and a basic linguistic module which represents mental expressions formed by syntactic rules and connects the other two modules.
claims.source: According to the psycholinguistic theory, the basic design of language faculty mainly comprises three modules (components): an external sensory-motor module, an internal conceptual-intentional module, and a basic linguistic module which represents mental expressions formed by syntactic rules and connects the other two modules (Berwick et al., 2013).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Berwick et al., 2013.

claims.claim: Flexible and adaptive cognitive functions arise from the dynamic brain, which transiently activates and coordinates distributed neural circuits in response to the changes in the external environment and internal demands.
claims.source: An emerging view suggests that flexible and adaptive cognitive functions arise from the dynamic brain, which transiently activates and coordinates distributed neural circuits in response to the changes in the external environment and internal demands (Honey et al., 2018; Kelso, 2012).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Honey et al., 2018 and Kelso, 2012.

claims.claim: The whole brain systematically switches among a limited number of temporal clusters or latent states with distinct spatial features during narrative comprehension or movie viewing.
claims.source: It has been found that the whole brain systematically switches among a limited number of temporal clusters or latent states with distinct spatial features.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by references to previous studies on narrative comprehension and movie viewing.

claims.claim: The switching of brain states was modulated by time-varying stimuli features including event boundary and movie annotations.
claims.source: Moreover, the switching of brain states was modulated by the time-varying stimuli features including event boundary (Baldassano et al., 2017) and movie annotations (van der Meer et al., 2020), and subjective experience including engagement (van der Meer et al., 2020), attention fluctuations (Song et al., 2023), emotional changes (Tan et al., 2022), and narrative integration (Song et al., 2021).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to previous studies.

claims.claim: The timescales of information accumulation vary hierarchically from early sensory areas to higher-order areas.
claims.source: Based on previous findings that the timescales of information accumulation vary hierarchically from early sensory areas to higher-order areas (Hasson et al., 2015; Lerner et al., 2011), we expect the occurrence probabilities of three brain states would be selectively modulated by these speech properties corresponding to distinct timescales.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Hasson et al., 2015 and Lerner et al., 2011.

claims.claim: Head movement serves as a reliable time-resolved indicator for task engagement, with greater task engagement accompanied by decreased movement.
claims.source: As an alternative, studies have demonstrated that head movement serves as a reliable time-resolved indicator for task engagement, with greater task engagement accompanied by decreased movement (Ballenghein et al., 2019; Greipl et al., 2021; Kaakinen et al., 2018).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Ballenghein et al., 2019; Greipl et al., 2021; and Kaakinen et al., 2018.

claims.claim: State #1 seems to be associated with the external sensory-motor module of language faculty.
claims.source: This state seems to be associated with the external sensory-motor module of language faculty.
claims.evidence: This is an interpretation based on the observed activity patterns of State #1.

claims.claim: State #2 seems to be associated with the basic linguistic component.
claims.source: The second state (State #2) was characterized by relatively high activities in the language and the frontal-parietal networks whereas low activities in the somatomotor and auditory networks, seemingly being associated with the basic linguistic component.
claims.evidence: This is an interpretation based on the observed activity patterns of State #2.

claims.claim: State #3 seems to be associated with the internal conceptual-intentional component.
claims.source: The third state (State #3) was characterized by relatively high activities in the DMN and frontal-parietal networks whereas low activities in the auditory and language networks, seemingly being associated with the internal conceptual-intentional component.
claims.evidence: This is an interpretation based on the observed activity patterns of State #3.

claims.claim: The tripartite state space likely captured some fundamental processes of the brain involved in narrative comprehension.
claims.source: The robustness of findings suggests the tripartite state space likely captured some fundamental processes of the brain involved in narrative comprehension.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the robustness of the findings across different datasets and parcellation schemes.

claims.claim: When occupied by State #2, the whole-brain networks were well connected to enable efficient information integration across distinct functional systems.
claims.source: These results indicate that, when occupied by State #2, the whole-brain networks were well connected to enable efficient information integration across distinct functional systems.
claims.evidence: This is an interpretation of the graph theoretical analysis results showing high global efficiency for State #2.

claims.claim: When occupied by State #1 and State #3, the whole-brain networks were well separated which enabled functional specialization.
claims.source: In contrast, when occupied by State #1 and State #3, the whole-brain networks were well separated which enabled functional specialization.
claims.evidence: This is an interpretation of the graph theoretical analysis results showing high modularity for State #1 and State #3.

claims.claim: Timely engagement with specific brain states, rather than the overall magnitude of engagement in those states, is crucial for narrative comprehension.
claims.source: Taken together, these findings suggest that timely engagement with specific brain states, rather than the overall magnitude of engagement in those states, is crucial for narrative comprehension.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the finding that ISC in state dynamics, but not FO or dwell time, predicted comprehension scores.

claims.claim: The lack of significant correlation between ISC and comprehension in older adults may be attributed to substantial heterogeneity among older adults arising from task-unrelated factors.
claims.source: This may be attributed to substantial heterogeneity among older adults arising from task-unrelated factors, which we tested by comparing the ISC between the two datasets.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the observation of lower ISC in older adults compared to younger adults.

claims.claim: The tripartite state space is not incidental, but likely reflects a fundamental principle governing the brain dynamics underlying narrative comprehension.
claims.source: A set of results convergently suggests that the tripartite state space is not incidental, but likely reflects a fundamental principle governing the brain dynamics underlying narrative comprehension.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the robustness and replicability of the tripartite state space findings.

claims.claim: The characteristics of the three latent states align well with the theoretical framework concerning the basic design of language faculty.
claims.source: Intriguingly, the characteristics of the three latent states align well with the theoretical framework concerning the basic design of language faculty (Berwick et al., 2013).
claims.evidence: This is an inference connecting the observed brain states to the theoretical language faculty model.

claims.claim: The cognitive processes underlying speech comprehension may not operate in parallel with equal priority or occur one after another, but instead one process dominates over others and this dominance changes over time, taking the form of mode-switching.
claims.source: Specifically, the time-varying probabilities of latent states indicate that the associated cognitive processes underlying speech comprehension may not operate in parallel with equal priority or occur one after another. Instead, while all processes are simultaneously engaged, one process dominates over others and this dominance changes over time, taking the form of mode-switching.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the observed dynamics of brain state expression probabilities.

claims.claim: Recruiting brain states in a timely manner is the key to effective speech comprehension.
claims.source: Furthermore, we found it was the alignment with the best performer (and the group-mean) in the time courses of state expression, rather than the overall occupancy of latent states, that positively correlated with participants' task performance, suggesting recruiting these states in a timely manner is the key to effective speech comprehension.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the correlation between ISC in state dynamics and comprehension scores.

claims.claim: For a given task, the brain follows modular organization where different regions specialize in specific functions, but the importance of these regions dynamically changes in response to external environment and internal demands.
claims.source: Specifically, for a given task, the brain follows modular organization where different regions specialize in specific functions. However, the importance of these regions dynamically changes in response to external environment and internal demands.
claims.evidence: This is a hypothesis proposed to reconcile modular and network approaches to understanding brain function.

claims.claim: Goal-directed behaviors arise from the precise temporal coordination of different functional modules.
claims.source: Accordingly, goal-directed behaviors arise from the precise temporal coordination of different functional modules (Vyas et al., 2020).
claims.evidence: This is a speculative claim supported by citation to Vyas et al., 2020.

claims.claim: The brain underlies narrative comprehension by switching through a tripartite state space, with each state probably dedicated to a specific component of language faculty.
claims.source: Our study suggests that the brain underlies narrative comprehension by switching through a tripartite state space, with each state probably dedicated to a specific component of language faculty, and effective narrative comprehension relies on engaging those states in a timely manner.
claims.evidence: This is the main conclusion of the study, integrating multiple findings.

claims.claim: Effective narrative comprehension relies on engaging brain states in a timely manner.
claims.source: Our study suggests that the brain underlies narrative comprehension by switching through a tripartite state space, with each state probably dedicated to a specific component of language faculty, and effective narrative comprehension relies on engaging those states in a timely manner.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion based on the correlation between ISC in state dynamics and comprehension scores.

claims.source: This research was approved by the Reviewer Board of Beijing Normal University in China (ICBIR_A_0002_009).

claims.evidence: This is a statement about the fMRI acquisition parameters.

claims.claim: The network detection approach identified a total of 11 networks, with two networks discarded due to comprising too few nodes (less than three), resulting in nine networks included for further analyses.
claims.source: The network detection approach identified a total of 11 networks (Figure 1—figure supplement 1). Two networks were discarded due to comprising too few nodes (less than three) and thus nine networks were included for further analyses.
claims.evidence: This is a statement about the brain parcellation results.

claims.claim: The nine networks were tentatively labeled as the auditory, visual, somatomotor, bilateral language, medial temporal, frontal-parietal, ventral attention, subcortical, and default mode networks.
claims.source: By reference to the functional decoding results using NeuroSynth (https://www.neurosynth.org), we tentatively labeled the nine networks as the auditory, visual, somatomotor, bilateral language, medial temporal, frontal-parietal, ventral attention, subcortical, and default mode networks.
claims.evidence: This is a statement about the labeling of brain networks based on functional decoding.

claims.claim: The HMM assumes that the observed data is generated through a finite number of latent states, and each state can be characterized, respectively, by a multivariate Gaussian distribution with mean and covariance.
claims.source: The HMM assumes that the observed data is generated through a finite number of latent states, and each state can be characterized, respectively, by a multivariate Gaussian distribution with mean and covariance.
claims.evidence: This is a statement about the mathematical assumptions of the HMM method.

claims.claim: Word-level semantic coherence was evaluated using cosine similarity between embedding vectors for each word and the preceding word.
claims.source: Word-level semantic coherence was evaluated using cosine similarity between embedding vectors for each word and the preceding word.
claims.evidence: This is a statement about the method used to measure word-level semantic coherence.

claims.claim: Clause-level semantic coherence was evaluated using cosine similarity between embedding vectors for each clause and the preceding clause.
claims.source: Clause-level semantic coherence was evaluated using cosine similarity between embedding vectors for each clause and the preceding clause.
claims.evidence: This is a statement about the method used to measure clause-level semantic coherence.

claims.claim: The low correlation between individual brain state dynamics and speech features (group averaged r ≈ 0.03) is likely due to the high level of noise inherent in fMRI data.
claims.source: We noted that the correlation value between individual brain state dynamics and speech features was relatively low (group averaged r ≈ 0.03), which is also the case in previous studies (e.g. Fernandino et al., 2022; Oota et al., 2022). This low correlation is likely due to the high level of noise inherent in fMRI data.
claims.evidence: This is an explanation for the observed low correlation values, supported by citations to previous studies.

claims.claim: Brain activity fluctuations are shaped by a variety of factors, including task-related cognitive processing, internal thoughts, physiological states, as well as arousal and vigilance.
claims.source: Brain activity fluctuations are shaped by a variety of factors, including task-related cognitive processing, internal thoughts, physiological states, as well as arousal and vigilance.
claims.evidence: This is a statement about factors influencing brain activity, based on general neuroscience knowledge.

claims.claim: The speech features measured may account for only a small portion of the cognitive processes underlying the task.
claims.source: Additionally, the speech features we measured may account for only a small portion of the cognitive processes underlying the task.
claims.evidence: This is an acknowledgment of the limitations of the speech feature measurements.

claims.claim: The variance in speech features may only explain a limited portion of the overall variance in brain state fluctuations.
claims.source: As a result, the variance in speech features may only explain a limited portion of the overall variance in brain state fluctuations.
claims.evidence: This is an inference about the explanatory power of speech features for brain state variance.

claims.claim: The inter-subject alignments in brain states were unlikely merely the byproduct of shared levels of task engagement, but instead reflected the commonality in neural processes that directly influence narrative comprehension.
claims.source: These findings suggest that the inter-subject alignments in brain states were unlikely merely the byproduct of shared levels of task engagement, but instead reflected the commonality in neural processes that directly influence narrative comprehension.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the partial correlation analysis controlling for head movement.

claims.claim: Despite engaging in the same task, older adults exhibit considerable inter-subject variation in cortical morphology, function, and brain metabolism.
claims.source: Despite engaging in the same task, older adults exhibit considerable inter-subject variation in cortical morphology, function, and brain metabolism (Yu, 2024).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Yu, 2024.

claims.claim: The activity patterns of the brain's latent states associated with each of the theoretical components of language faculty are consistent with the findings from earlier studies that have mainly focused on the averaged brain activities over time.
claims.source: The activity patterns of the brain's latent states associated with each of the theoretical components of language faculty are consistent with the findings from earlier studies that have mainly focused on the averaged brain activities over time (Ferstl et al., 2008; Price, 2012).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Ferstl et al., 2008 and Price, 2012.

claims.source: The modular approach postulates the brain areas to act as independent processors for a specific aspect of complex cognitive functions, contributing to much of our current knowledge of the relationship between the brain and behavior.

results.result: The study collected fMRI data from 64 young adults (after exclusions) listening to 10-minute Chinese narratives and 50 runs from 30 older adults listening to Chinese dialect narratives. Standard fMRI acquisition parameters and ethical procedures were followed.
results.evaluation: Claims C1-C4 and C61-C64 provide clear documentation of participant demographics, exclusion criteria, scanning parameters, and ethical approvals. The methodological details are explicit and standard for fMRI studies, supporting the validity of the dataset.

results.result: Hidden Markov Modeling with K=3 states optimally characterized brain dynamics during narrative comprehension, as demonstrated by highest combined clustering performance and narrative classification accuracy. This tripartite organization was robust across different brain parcellation schemes and generalizable to an older adult dataset.
results.evaluation: Claims C5-C7 provide convergent evidence from multiple analyses (different parcellations, different age groups) that K=3 is optimal. The composite scoring approach combining clustering and classification (C5) is methodologically sound. Claims C47 and C53 appropriately interpret this robustness as evidence for fundamental processes.

results.result: Three distinct brain states were identified with characteristic spatial patterns: State #1 (high auditory/somatomotor activity), State #2 (high language/frontal-parietal activity), and State #3 (high DMN/frontal-parietal activity). These states align with theoretical language faculty components: external sensory-motor, basic linguistic, and internal conceptual-intentional modules, respectively.
results.evaluation: Claims C8-C10 provide explicit data-driven characterizations of the three states shown in Figure 2. Claims C44-C46 and C54 appropriately link these empirical patterns to theoretical frameworks (Berwick et al., 2013), though the interpretations are acknowledged as tentative ('seems to be associated'). The alignment is conceptually coherent and supported by the spatial patterns.

results.result: State #2 acts as a transitional hub, with States #1 and #3 more likely to transition to State #2 than to each other. The brain spent the most time in State #2 (46.7% fractional occupancy, 15.29s dwell time), with these metrics significantly exceeding surrogate data distributions.
results.evaluation: Claims C11-C15 provide converging evidence for State #2's hub role through transition probabilities (C11-C12), fractional occupancy (C13, C15), and dwell time (C14-C15). The permutation testing against surrogate data (C12, C15) provides statistical rigor, with observed values exceeding 94.4-99.9% of null distributions.

results.result: State #2 exhibited significantly higher global efficiency and lower modularity than States #1 and #3, indicating that when occupied by State #2, whole-brain networks enable efficient information integration, while States #1 and #3 enable functional specialization.
results.evaluation: Claims C16-C17 provide statistical evidence (t>4.67, p<10^-4 for efficiency; t<-5.82, p<10^-6 for modularity) from graph theoretical analyses. Claims C48-C49 appropriately interpret these topological properties in terms of integration vs. specialization. The analyses were conducted using both individual-level and HMM-derived connectivity matrices, enhancing robustness.

results.result: Brain state expression probabilities were selectively modulated by narrative properties at different timescales: speech envelope modulated States #1 and #2, word-level semantic coherence modulated State #2, and clause-level semantic coherence modulated State #3. Correlations were modest (r≈0.03) but statistically significant and exceeded permutation-based null distributions.
results.evaluation: Claims C18-C23 provide statistical evidence for selective modulation effects with appropriate corrections (FDR) and permutation testing. Claims C68-C69 document the methods for measuring semantic coherence. Claims C70-C73 acknowledge and explain the low correlation magnitudes, citing fMRI noise and the limited explanatory scope of measured features. The selective pattern (different states responding to different timescales) is the key finding, not the absolute correlation magnitude.

results.result: Inter-subject alignment in brain state dynamics (but not overall state occupancy) predicted narrative comprehension performance. Alignment with best performers correlated with comprehension for States #1 (r=0.31) and #2 (r=0.37), and alignment with group-mean correlated for all states (r=0.27-0.51). These effects remained significant after controlling for head movement, indicating they reflect neural processes rather than task engagement.
results.evaluation: Claims C24-C26 provide correlation evidence linking inter-subject alignment to comprehension. Claim C27 establishes head movement as a proxy for engagement. Claim C28 shows the critical partial correlation analysis controlling for head movement, with effects remaining significant for States #1-2. Claim C29 shows no relationship between FO/dwell time and comprehension, supporting the interpretation that timing (C50, C56, C60) rather than magnitude matters. Claim C74 appropriately interprets the partial correlation results.

results.result: In the older adult dataset, inter-subject alignment in brain states did not significantly correlate with comprehension, likely due to substantial heterogeneity in this population. Inter-subject correlations were significantly lower in older adults compared to younger adults for all three states.
results.evaluation: Claims C30-C31 document the null finding in older adults and the significantly lower ISC values (all p≤0.001). Claims C51 and C75 provide a reasonable explanation for the null result based on age-related heterogeneity. While the lack of replication in older adults is a limitation, the authors appropriately acknowledge and explain it rather than overgeneralizing from the young adult findings.

results.result: Comparison across conditions (rest, unintelligible speech, narrative comprehension) revealed that State #3 was the transitional hub during rest, while State #2 remained the hub during unintelligible speech. State #2 fractional occupancy increased monotonically (rest < unintelligible < comprehension) while State #3 decreased, indicating the tripartite state space is driven by language processing.
results.evaluation: Claims C32-C36 provide systematic comparison across three conditions with progressively increasing linguistic demands. The monotonic changes in fractional occupancy and dwell time (C34-C36) for States #2 and #3 provide strong evidence that these states are specifically related to language processing rather than being task-free intrinsic organization. The shift in transitional hub from State #3 (rest) to State #2 (language conditions) further supports this interpretation.

results.result: A data-driven network detection approach identified 11 networks from the Brainnetome atlas, with 9 networks retained after excluding those with fewer than 3 nodes. These were labeled as auditory, visual, somatomotor, bilateral language, medial temporal, frontal-parietal, ventral attention, subcortical, and default mode networks based on NeuroSynth functional decoding.
results.evaluation: Claims C65-C66 document the brain parcellation procedure using established methods (Ji et al., 2019) with appropriate quality control criteria. The use of NeuroSynth for functional labeling is standard practice. The resulting 9-network parcellation provides the foundation for subsequent HMM analyses.

results.result: The study is grounded in established theoretical frameworks: speech comprehension involves multiple interacting cognitive processes (C37), language faculty comprises three modules (C38), flexible cognition arises from dynamic brain networks (C39-C41), information processing occurs at hierarchical timescales (C42), and head movement indexes task engagement (C43).
results.evaluation: Claims C37-C43 appropriately cite relevant prior work to establish the theoretical and empirical foundations for the study. These are well-established principles in cognitive neuroscience and psycholinguistics, properly attributed to original sources (Berwick et al., 2013; Honey et al., 2018; Hasson et al., 2015; etc.).

results.result: The study proposes that cognitive processes underlying speech comprehension operate through mode-switching where one process dominates at a time (C55), reconciling modular and network approaches by suggesting that functional modules dynamically change in importance (C57-C58). The brain underlies narrative comprehension by switching through a tripartite state space dedicated to specific language components (C59).
results.evaluation: Claims C55 and C57-C59 present the study's main theoretical contributions, integrating the empirical findings into a coherent framework. These interpretations are well-supported by the convergent evidence from state characterization, transition patterns, stimulus modulation, and behavioral correlations. Claim C58 appropriately cites supporting work (Vyas et al., 2020). The framework provides a mechanistic account bridging modular and dynamic network perspectives.

results.result: The HMM assumes observed data is generated through a finite number of latent states, each characterized by a multivariate Gaussian distribution with mean and covariance.
results.evaluation: Claim C67 accurately describes the mathematical assumptions of the HMM method used in the study. This is a standard description of HMM methodology.

results.result: The study's findings are consistent with prior literature on language networks (C76), and the work addresses longstanding debates between modular (C77-C78) and network (C79) approaches to brain function. The dataset has been used in previous publications (C80) and materials are publicly available (C81).
results.evaluation: Claims C76-C81 appropriately contextualize the findings within existing literature and document data provenance and availability. These claims support transparency and reproducibility.

results.result: The authors identified three brain states (K=3) as optimal during narrative comprehension using Hidden Markov Modeling. This finding was robust across different brain parcellation schemes (Yeo-7 Networks atlas) and replicated in an independent dataset of older adults with different narrative content and scanning duration.
results.evaluation: Reviewers explicitly affirmed this finding as a strength. One reviewer noted 'the authors repeated the HMM analyses across different tasks (Figure 5) and an independent dataset (Figure S3) and found that the data was consistently best fit by 3 brain states.' The editor summarized that the study 'provides important insights into the brain activity and connectivity underlying speech comprehension, revealing three brain states.'

results.result: The three brain states showed distinct spatial activity patterns that align with theoretical components of language faculty: State #1 (auditory/somatomotor networks - sensory-motor module), State #2 (language/frontal-parietal networks - linguistic module), and State #3 (DMN/frontal-parietal networks - conceptual-intentional module).
results.evaluation: While reviewers acknowledged the theoretical grounding, one reviewer raised concerns about the interpretation, noting that 'a "single-process" account where the states differ in terms of the temporal window for which one needs to integrate information over may offer a more parsimonious account than a multi-process account where the states correspond to distinct processes.' The reviewer stated this alternative interpretation 'is mentioned briefly in the introduction, but not developed further,' suggesting the functional role of states 'remains under-explored.'

results.result: State #2 acts as a transitional hub between States #1 and #3, with both states more likely to transition to State #2 than directly to each other. State #2 also showed the highest fractional occupancy (46.7%) and longest dwelling time (15.29s), significantly exceeding surrogate data expectations.
results.evaluation: Reviewers accepted these findings without critique. One reviewer explicitly noted that 'States 1 and 3 were more likely to transition to State 2 than between one another, suggesting that State 2 acts as a transition hub between states.' The statistical validation against surrogate data was not questioned.

results.result: State #2 exhibited significantly higher global efficiency and lower modularity compared to States #1 and #3, indicating that State #2 enables efficient information integration across functional systems while States #1 and #3 enable functional specialization.
results.evaluation: Reviewers did not challenge these network topology findings. The interpretation that State #2 enables integration while other states enable specialization was implicitly accepted as part of the overall characterization of the three states.

results.result: Brain state expression probabilities correlated with hierarchical speech features: State #1 with speech envelope (acoustic), State #2 with word-level semantic coherence, and State #3 with clause-level semantic coherence. However, correlations were relatively low (~0.03), which the authors attribute to fMRI noise and speech features accounting for only a small portion of cognitive processes.
results.evaluation: Reviewers explicitly acknowledged these findings as an important contribution. One reviewer stated 'An important contribution of this paper is that it relates the expression of brain states to specific features of the stimulus in a manner that is consistent with theoretical predictions.' The same reviewer noted 'The correlation between narrative features and brain state expression was reliable, but relatively low (~0.03). As discussed in the manuscript, this could be due to measurement noise, as well as narrative features accounting for a small proportion of cognitive processes underlying the brain states.'

results.result: Inter-subject alignment in brain state dynamics (not overall state occupancy) correlated with narrative comprehension scores. Alignment with best performers in States #1 and #2 significantly predicted comprehension even after controlling for head movement, suggesting timely engagement with brain states is crucial for effective comprehension.
results.evaluation: Reviewers affirmed this as a key finding. One reviewer noted 'Participants whose brain state trajectories closely matched those of an individual with high comprehension scores tended to have higher comprehension scores themselves, suggesting that optimal transitions between brain states facilitated narrative comprehension.' The editor highlighted that the study successfully linked 'brain state dynamics to comprehension scores.'

results.result: In the older adult replication dataset, no significant correlations were found between inter-subject alignment in brain states and comprehension. ISCs were significantly lower in older adults compared to younger adults for all three states, which the authors attribute to substantial heterogeneity among older adults from task-unrelated factors.
results.evaluation: Reviewers did not challenge these findings. The lack of correlation in older adults and the explanation based on heterogeneity were accepted as reported, though not extensively discussed in the reviews.

results.result: Brain state organization varied across conditions: during rest, State #3 acted as the transitional hub (unlike during narrative comprehension); during incomprehensible speech (Mongolian), State #2 remained the hub. State #2 fractional occupancy increased monotonically (rest < incomprehensible < comprehension) while State #3 decreased monotonically.
results.evaluation: Reviewers acknowledged these cross-task comparisons as a strength. One reviewer noted 'the authors repeated the HMM analyses across different tasks (Figure 5)' and observed that 'Across tasks, however, the spatial regions associated with each state varied. For example, state 2 during narrative comprehension was similar to both states 2 and 3 during rest (Fig. 5A), suggesting that the organization of the three states was task dependent.'

results.result: The study used two datasets: 68 Chinese college students (64 after exclusions) listening to Chinese narratives, and 30 older adults (50 runs after exclusions) as replication. Standard fMRI acquisition and preprocessing methods were employed, with brain parcellation identifying nine functional networks.
results.evaluation: Reviewers did not raise concerns about the datasets, sample sizes, or methodological procedures. The methods were implicitly accepted as appropriate for the study's aims.

results.result: The study is grounded in theoretical frameworks including the tripartite language faculty model (sensory-motor, linguistic, conceptual-intentional modules), dynamic brain perspectives, and prior findings on brain state switching during naturalistic tasks and hierarchical timescales of information processing.
results.evaluation: Reviewers praised the theoretical grounding. One reviewer stated 'I appreciated the way the authors theoretically grounded their hypotheses and reviewed relevant papers that used the HMM on other naturalistic datasets.' Another noted 'The authors cleverly used the HMM to test the external/linguistic/internal processing theory that was suggested in comprehension literature.'

results.result: The authors conclude that the tripartite state space reflects a fundamental principle of brain dynamics underlying narrative comprehension, with each state dedicated to a specific language faculty component, and that effective comprehension relies on timely state engagement.
results.evaluation: While reviewers acknowledged the conclusions are 'well-supported by the data,' one reviewer suggested an alternative interpretation: 'a "single-process" account where the states differ in terms of the temporal window for which one needs to integrate information over may offer a more parsimonious account than a multi-process account.' The editor noted 'the functional role of these states remains under-explored,' indicating the interpretation requires further development.

results.result: The authors propose that cognitive processes underlying speech comprehension operate through mode-switching where one process dominates over others at different times, reconciling modular and network approaches by suggesting brain regions dynamically change in importance while maintaining modular organization.
results.evaluation: Reviewers did not explicitly critique this theoretical synthesis. The proposal was implicitly accepted as a reasonable interpretation of the findings, though not extensively discussed in the reviews.

comparisons.comparison: Both evaluate the K=3 optimal state finding (C5-C7). OpenEval rates as SUPPORTED, emphasizing convergent evidence and methodological soundness. Peer reviewers also rate SUPPORTED, explicitly affirming this as a strength with validation across tasks and datasets.

Both address state characterization and theoretical interpretation (C8-C10, C44-C46, C54). OpenEval rates SUPPORTED, noting conceptual coherence with tentative interpretations. Peer reviewers rate UNCERTAIN, raising concerns about alternative 'single-process' accounts and suggesting the functional role remains under-explored.

Both evaluate State #2's hub role (C11-C15). OpenEval rates SUPPORTED, highlighting converging evidence from transition probabilities, fractional occupancy, and statistical validation. Peer reviewers also rate SUPPORTED without critique, explicitly acknowledging the transition hub finding.

Both assess network topology findings (C16-C17, C48-C49). OpenEval rates SUPPORTED, noting statistical evidence and appropriate interpretation of integration vs. specialization. Peer reviewers also rate SUPPORTED, implicitly accepting these characterizations without challenge.

Both evaluate stimulus modulation findings (C18-C23, C70-C73). OpenEval rates SUPPORTED, emphasizing selective patterns and acknowledging low correlation magnitudes with explanations. Peer reviewers also rate SUPPORTED, explicitly noting this as an important contribution and accepting the low correlation explanation.

Both assess behavioral correlations with comprehension (C24-C29, C50, C56, C60, C74). OpenEval rates SUPPORTED, highlighting partial correlation controls and timing-based interpretation. Peer reviewers also rate SUPPORTED, affirming this as a key finding linking state dynamics to comprehension.

Both evaluate older adult findings (C30-C31, C51, C75). OpenEval rates SUPPORTED, noting appropriate acknowledgment of null results and heterogeneity explanation. Peer reviewers also rate SUPPORTED, accepting the findings and explanation without challenge.

Both assess cross-task validation (C32-C36). OpenEval rates SUPPORTED, emphasizing monotonic changes and evidence for language-specific processing. Peer reviewers also rate SUPPORTED, acknowledging cross-task analyses as a strength while noting task-dependent spatial organization.

Both evaluate methodological documentation (C1-C4, C61-C66). OpenEval rates SUPPORTED for demographics, scanning parameters, and parcellation procedures. Peer reviewers also rate SUPPORTED, implicitly accepting methods as appropriate without raising concerns.

Both assess theoretical grounding and literature citations (C37-C43, C76-C79). OpenEval rates SUPPORTED, noting appropriate attribution of established principles. Peer reviewers also rate SUPPORTED, praising theoretical grounding and hypothesis development.

Both evaluate theoretical synthesis (C55, C57-C58). OpenEval rates SUPPORTED, noting integration of empirical findings into coherent framework. Peer reviewers also rate SUPPORTED, implicitly accepting the interpretation without extensive critique.

Partial overlap on interpretive claims (C47, C53, C59). OpenEval R2 rates SUPPORTED for robustness interpretation. Peer R11 rates UNCERTAIN, suggesting alternative single-process accounts may be more parsimonious and noting functional roles remain under-explored.
